newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chernomyrdin vows shake-up in Russia government.
newsitem.headline: Chernomyrdin vows shake-up in Russia government.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin vowed on Thursday to reshuffle his government and singled out the Finance Ministry for criticism.

His comments at a cabinet meeting following President Boris Yeltsin's annual state of the nation address also appeared to prepare the ground for a return to government by liberal reformers and notably Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais.

Official sources said Chubais was almost certainly to become Chernomyrdin's number two. Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin sources saying Yeltsin would sign a decree on Friday naming Chubais first deputy prime minister overseeing economic reforms.

Chubais, architect of Russia's post-Soviet privatisation programme, is loathed by Yeltsin's communist and nationalist opponents in parliament, who accuse the 41-year-old economist of personally profiting from the sell-offs. He denies the charges.
Earlier on Thursday, Chubais said Yeltsin had not yet decided whether to parachute him into the government.
Chernomyrdin told the cabinet he was planning an overhaul of the way his government conducted business in order to implement reforms and reduce bureaucratic interference in the economy.

"The time has come to concentrate on the most essential questions -- to change the style of the government's work, its structure and personal composition. We will act decisively and systematically," the premier said.

Chernomyrdin, who last restructured his team only in August, was echoing Yeltsin, who told parliament in the morning that the composition and structure of the government would be changed and new appointments announced in the next few days.
Neither Yeltsin nor Chernomyrdin said who would be involved in the changes.
But Chernomyrdin said the Finance Ministry should not be the dominant body in economic policy and the role of the Economy Ministry in this area should be strengthened.

"The Economy Ministry should be the headquarters of the country's economic policy," he told the cabinet. "Here is where the conception of the budget and the development of federal programmes will begin."
Chernomyrdin said the Economy Ministry should not be less powerful than the Finance Ministry, which was displaying excessive bureaucracy and arrogance towards the regions and other ministries.

The premier said he wanted to end some ministries, hangovers from Soviet days of comprehensive central planning, which are responsible for specific industrial sectors, many of which have now been almost entirely privatised.
His remarks suggested a return to a government model first propagated by reformers last summer that envisaged a tighter cabinet team with fewer tiers of responsibility.
The government currently has 12 deputy prime ministers, including three first deputies. Kremlin sources say Chubais is likely to be the only first deputy after the reshuffle.

In Russia's largely privatised, post-communist economy, there was still too much government meddling in different sectors, with officials often turning into lobbyists for the industry under their supervision, Chernomyrdin said.
"At the end of the 20th century, can people still fail to understand that the command economy is a direct path to lawlessness and poverty," he said.
